newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ business, unions attack govt spending plans.
newsitem.headline: NZ business, unions attack govt spending plans.

text.p: Big business, manufacturers and trade union groups on Wednesday criticised the New Zealand government's spending plans at a hearing of parliament's finance and expenditure committee (FEC).

In submissions during the committee's consideration of the Budget Policy Statement, big business lobby groups -- the Business Roundtable and the Manufacturers' Federation -- criticised the level and quality of planned spending while the Council of Trade Unions (CTU) said the extra NZ$5 billion extra spending over three years was unfair.

Business Roundtable executive director Roger Kerr said the policy statement, which outlined the government's broad fiscal plans and was tabled by Treasurer Winston Peters in March, increased spending at a rate not seen since the era of former Prime Minister Rob Muldoon in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
He said the extra spending was putting increasing pressure on the economy, but he said the 3.0 percent to 3.5 percent annual growth rate projected by Treasury was possible, although at the high end.
"We think there could be some downside risk," Kerr said.
He said the level of planned spending was imprudent.
"It's putting the gains that the Government has seen in recent years at risk," he said.
Kerr said the Government's spending priorities were also "rather perverse", by targeting higher income earners, a point echoed by CTU economist Peter Harris.

Manufacturers' Federation chief executive Simon Arnold said the increased spending was pushing up inflation, and the federation would continue to argue against a planned $100 million boost to business.
He said inflation was also being fuelled by the impact on house prices of a move to market rents for state tenants.
In their submission mnaufacturers warned of a return to the "boom-bust" cycle that characterised the economy in the 1970s and early 1980s.
Harris of the CTU said the spending plans were based on optimistic economic growth forecasts with no fall back position.

"The income and expenditure account is an overly optimistic projection for economic growth, but more importantly there is no 'Plan B', no idea of how the government would reinvigorate the economy. It is a fair weather document," Harris said.

He said planned extra spending was "clearly inequitable" and the debate over whether there should be spending or tax cuts amounted to a family squabble within the National Party over whether the children or the parents should get most.
There was an urgent need to deal with social stresses in areas such as housing, but the policy statement did not address these needs.
"It's got nothing to do with low and middle income families and everything to do with political posturing," he said.
The Budget is due to be delivered in June.
